components.html:
Ponchos are timeless alternatives to sweaters. Easy on / easy off warmth they are a perfect project if you are just getting started with your knitting machine, or if you are ready to spread your wings and try new-to-you techniques.
Play with yarn and stitch patterns, add designer touches ... use the basic rectangle shapes as a canvas for your creativity.
No matter where you are on your journey, from the all-important planning stage to finishing, this course will help you gain confidence with your machine and you will end up with more than just swatches.
The goal of this knit-along is for you to have success.
Please work to your current skill level
and build your confidence with a finished poncho that you can be proud of!

Be honest with yourself. Approach this project based on where you are on your journey to master your machine.
  • Just getting started? Stick to Level 1 tasks.

  • Feeling adventurous? Add more challenges for yourself.

ALL LEVELS
1
PLAN
  • What yarn are you going to use? (Be sure it's an appropriate weight for your machine) Yarn refresher
  • Size: Who are you knitting for? The Poncho pattern has some suggested dimensions, but you can make this any size you like
  • Finishing: How are you going to finish the edges? Crochet? I-Cord? No finish?

SWATCH
  • Using the garment yarn, knit a "proper" swatch
  • Dress it and treat it as you will treat the finished poncho
  • Visit the swatching classroom

HOW MUCH YARN? Determine if you have enough yarn:
  • Use the built-in calculator in the pattern. After you've build your pattern click the icon to use the estimator
  • If aren't using yarn from your stash, here are some tips.

GET KNITTING
  • Making all your choices BEFORE you start knitting will prevent headaches later. Record your plan in the next section

Your success with this course AND your success with your knitting machine depends on your understanding and mastering the art of knitting gauge swatches.
Without a swatch we are knitting in the dark.
  • How is the final sweater going to feel in the yarn and stitch pattern you've chosen?
  • Do you have enough yarn?
  • Do you have enough needles on your machine for the size you chose?

blocks.title: Step 1: Your Success Depends on this

components.html:
If you haven't used your chosen yarn before, how do you know the best tension to knit your poncho? 
Knitters tend to use the terms "tension swatch" and "gauge swatch" interchangeably, lets take a look at both.

GAUGE SWATCH

The gauge swatch is the "official" swatch used when designing a garment.
It is knit at a specific size, marked for accurate stitch and row measurement and "dressed" as the final garment will be treated.
TIP: Whatever method you use to create a swatch, the key is to correctly measure it and calculate your gauge.

TENSION SWATCH

When I pick up a new cone of yarn, I can't wait to thread up my machine and see what the yarn looks like.   From the initial cast on, I start guessing what setting on my tension dial I need to use.  I knit a few inches and reach down and start to feel the resulting fabric.
Once I get a feel for the yarn (what machine, general tension setting at stockinette, etc) I create a tension swatch.  This helps me fine-tune the tension needed to achieve the fabric I like and allows me to play with various techniques.  I'm often very surprised that a yarn looks great in tuck, and awful in slip, for example.  Adding a few eyelets here and there tells me if the yarn will work up in lace.
Let's practice knitting a tension swatch.

1. Play!
  2. Start knitting stockenette at the tightest tension that will knit.  (If the tension is too tight, you'll see stitches that don't form properly.
  3. Knit 2-4 inches. Knit a marker row (change colors, work a few eyelets across the row or knit a sewing thread in with the main yarn)
  4. Keep knitting sections, marking the tension dial number in each section.  Knit the last section as loosely as possiblle, even if you think this will be too loose ... I'm often very pleasantly surprised at the result.
  5. Transfer every other needle to out of work postion and knit a section - put all needles back into work.
  6. Work a simple tuck, or slip, or any stitch pattern of your choice ... base your tension dial setting on the stockinette sections you just knit.
The point of this exercise is to put the yarn through it's paces ... ignite your creativity, and get a feel for what the yarn can do.  If you don't have a huge cone, you can always re-wind this knitting. At this point, you probably know exactly what you want to do with this yarn.  Knit your Gauge Swatch, dress it and and you are ready to design and knit your sweater.

Hand knitters use the excuse "It takes too much time to knit a swatch", then they are often disappointed that their knitting doesn't fit.
Machine knitters, rejoice!  Knitting a swatch is fast and the information it supplies is invaluable ...even for something as simple as a rectangle.

Time to get knitting!
  1. Knit a swatch using any method.
  2. Let it rest
  3. Dress the swatch (treat it as you will treat your blanket)
  4. Accurately measure YOUR stitch and row gauge
  5. Record your gauge below

Classroom: Cast on Methods Classroom: Bind Off Methods

Every knitter has their own opinions about blocking. About the only thing they can agree on is the fact that blocking can improve the finished appearance of our knitting. The methods of blocking vary from knitter to knitter.

Steam

Using steam with a steam iron or a dedicate steamer is a popular way to "set" the knitting.
  • Lay the knitting on a flat, protected surface and gently steam. (Be extra careful with man-made fibers, steam, don't iron)

  • Pin the knitting to a flat surface with or without Blocking Wires and gently steam

Wet Blocking

Another popular method of blocking is to wash the knitting (if appropriate for your fiber). This cleans the item as well as blocking it.
  • With the piece towel dried, gently lay it on a protected surface and let it dry

  • Use blocking wires if desired, pin the piece into shape and let dry
Although blocking can be used to shape the knitting and adjust the size, it is not a replacement for knitting the garment to the correct size.
Accurate gauge measurement and garment planning is preferable to stretching and forcing a piece to size with any blocking method.
